Theorem E.11

(Markov’s theorem
[
45
]
)
.

Let
K_{1},K_{2}
be two oriented links which can be formed from the braids
\beta_{1},\beta_{2}
, respectively. Then
K_{1}\sim{K_{2}}\Leftrightarrow\beta_{1}\sim_{M}\beta_{2}
.

For a proof of this; see Birman’s survey
[
12
, pp. 18–26]
or Birman’s original paper
[
10
]
.

E.I
Motivation

Since we have reached the end of the first part, we will summarise and thus motivate the second part with all of what we learned here.

Alexander’s theorem
E.3
says that all links have a braid representation, and Markov’s theorem
E.11
says that two links are equivalent if and only if their braid representations are Markov equivalent (i.e., they can be transformed by
M1
and
M2
moves). So, then we call the
Markov braid type
the infinite union of the braid group
\mathcal{B}_{\infty}
that is quotiented by the two Markov moves (Markov equivalence). And so we have,

\{\text{link type}\}\simeq\{\text{Markov braid type}\}

So if we prove that a function is invariant under the Markov moves, then by Markov’s theorem we have that it is a link invariant.
And this will be the strategy for the upcoming original construction of the Jones polynomial (See Chapter
H
).

More precisely, for
a\in\mathcal{B}_{n}
and any
i<n
, we have
\hbox{\hskip 451.29065pt\hskip-2.64294pt\hbox{$a$}\hskip-2.64294pt\hskip-451.29065pt\raisebox{15.30566pt}{\hbox{$\hbox{\raisebox{-3.34055pt}{\resizebox{53617400}{141084}{\hbox{\raisebox{10.00012pt}{$\mathchoice{\raisebox{-853.45891pt}{\resizebox{468892385}{36044800}{\hbox{\raisebox{10.00012pt}{$\displaystyle\mathchoice{\raisebox{0.0pt}{\resizebox{0}{0}{\hbox{\raisebox{10.00012pt}{$\displaystyle\kern-0.6pt\bigwedge\kern-0.6pt$}}}}}{\raisebox{0.0pt}{\resizebox{0}{0}{\hbox{\raisebox{10.00012pt}{$\textstyle\kern-0.6pt\bigwedge\kern-0.6pt$}}}}}{\raisebox{0.0pt}{\resizebox{0}{0}{\hbox{\raisebox{1.4pt}{$\scriptstyle\kern-0.6pt\bigwedge\kern-0.6pt$}}}}}{\raisebox{0.0pt}{\resizebox{0}{0}{\hbox{\raisebox{1.0pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle\kern-0.6pt\bigwedge\kern-0.6pt$}}}}}$}}}}}{\raisebox{-853.45891pt}{\resizebox{468892385}{36044800}{\hbox{\raisebox{10.00012pt}{$\textstyle\mathchoice{\raisebox{0.0pt}{\resizebox{0}{0}{\hbox{\raisebox{10.00012pt}{$\displaystyle\kern-0.6pt\bigwedge\kern-0.6pt$}}}}}{\raisebox{0.0pt}{\resizebox{0}{0}{\hbox{\raisebox{10.00012pt}{$\textstyle\kern-0.6pt\bigwedge\kern-0.6pt$}}}}}{\raisebox{0.0pt}{\resizebox{0}{0}{\hbox{\raisebox{1.4pt}{$\scriptstyle\kern-0.6pt\bigwedge\kern-0.6pt$}}}}}{\raisebox{0.0pt}{\resizebox{0}{0}{\hbox{\raisebox{1.0pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle\kern-0.6pt\bigwedge\kern-0.6pt$}}}}}$}}}}}{\raisebox{-157.14236pt}{\resizebox{468892385}{36044800}{\hbox{\raisebox{1.4pt}{$\scriptstyle\mathchoice{\raisebox{0.0pt}{\resizebox{0}{0}{\hbox{\raisebox{1.4pt}{$\displaystyle\kern-0.6pt\bigwedge\kern-0.6pt$}}}}}{\raisebox{0.0pt}{\resizebox{0}{0}{\hbox{\raisebox{1.4pt}{$\textstyle\kern-0.6pt\bigwedge\kern-0.6pt$}}}}}{\raisebox{0.0pt}{\resizebox{0}{0}{\hbox{\raisebox{0.98pt}{$\scriptstyle\kern-0.6pt\bigwedge\kern-0.6pt$}}}}}{\raisebox{0.0pt}{\resizebox{0}{0}{\hbox{\raisebox{0.7pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle\kern-0.6pt\bigwedge\kern-0.6pt$}}}}}$}}}}}{\raisebox{-157.14285pt}{\resizebox{468892385}{36044800}{\hbox{\raisebox{1.0pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle\mathchoice{\raisebox{0.0pt}{\res . So our strategy of constructing the Jones polynomial will be to define a tracial function on the Temperley-Lieb algebra. Where the Temperley-Lieb algebra is seen as a quotient algebra of the group algebra
\mathbb{C}[\mathcal{B}_{n}]
. There exists other similar constructions, however for the purposes of this essay we will use the Temperley-Lieb algebras since it has a very comprehensible diagrammatic definition. To see other similar constructions; a very nice read is
[

]
. The following chapter will briefly touch on the work that Jones did in 1983

. We just want to see the correlation he made between the von Neumann algebras and constructing a link invariant.

F.I
Background

We shall first review some background we will need. The discussion in this section is mainly based on that in the author’s exposition on analysis
&
its foundations
[
54
]
.

A
norm
over a vector space
V
over
\mathbb{C}
is a map
\|\cdot\|:V\to\mathbb{R}
that satisfies

(i)

\|v\|\geq 0
, with equality if and only if
v=0
for all
v\in{V}

(ii)

\|\lambda{v}\|=|\lambda|\|v\|
for all
v\in{V}
and
\lambda\in\mathbb{C}

(iii)

\|v+w\|\leq\|v\|+\|w\|
for all
v,w\in{V}

A
normed vector space
is a vector space
V
over
\mathbb{C}
with a norm
\|\cdot\|
.
We say that a normed vector space is a
Banach space
if it is complete (i.e., any Cauchy sequence converges).
We call a map
\varphi:V\to\mathbb{C}
a
linear functional
if it satisfies
\varphi(\lambda{v}+\mu{w})=\lambda\varphi(v)+\mu\varphi(w)
, for all
\lambda,\mu\in\mathbb{C}
and
v,w\in{V}
. We say the linear functional is
bounded
if
\|\varphi\|=\sup_{\|x\|\leq 1}|\varphi(x)|<\infty
. The
dual
of the normed vector space
V
, is the normed vector space of all bounded linear functionals
\varphi:V\to\mathbb{C}
, and we denote it as
V^{*}
.

Now, we call a map
T:V\to{V}

linear
if it satisfies
T(\lambda{v}+\mu{w})=\lambda{T(v)}+\mu{T(w)}
for all
v,w\in\mathbb{C}
and
v,w\in{V}
. We call the linear map
bounded
if
\|T\|=\sup_{\|v\|\leq 1}\|T(v)\|<\infty
. We let
\mathbb{B}(V)
be the normed vector space of all bounded linear maps
T:V\to{V}
.

A
Hilbert space
is essentially a complete inner product on a vector space
V
over
\mathbb{C}
, i.e.,

\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle\colon{V\times{V}\to\mathbb{C}}

satisfying the following for all
x,y,z\in{V}
and
\lambda\in\mathbb{C}
,

(i)

\langle{x,y}\rangle=\overline{\langle{y,x}\rangle}

(ii)

\langle\lambda{x}+y,z\rangle=\lambda\langle{x,z}\rangle+\langle{y,z}\rangle

(iii)

\langle{x,x}\rangle\geq 0
with equality if and only if
x=0

Notice that if we let the norm
\|x\|=\sqrt{\langle{x,x}\rangle}
for any
x\in{V}
, then we can see
|\langle{x,y}\rangle|\leq\|x\|\|y\|
for any
x,y\in{V}
. This inequality is known as the
Cauchy-Shwarz inequality
(it is easy to show that this is indeed satisfied). So, in fact, an inner product induces a norm.

Notation.

Note that the notation used for the inner product
\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle
should not be confused with the Kauffman bracket
\langle\cdot\rangle
from the previous chapters. In fact, all notations used in this chapter are self-contained, unless stated otherwise.

The
adjoint
of an operator
T:\mathcal{H}\to\mathcal{H}^{\prime}
is the unique linear map
T^{*}:\mathcal{H}\to\mathcal{H}
such that for all
x\in\mathcal{H}^{\prime}
and
y\in\mathcal{H}
we have
\langle{T^{*}x,y}\rangle=\langle{x,Ty}\rangle
.

An
algebra
is a vector space
V
over
\mathbb{C}
if there is a multiplication operation
V\times{V}\to{V}
, given by
(u,v)\mapsto{uv}
such that for all
u,v,w\in{V}
and
\lambda,\mu\in\mathbb{C}
, we have
u(v+w)=uv+uw
,
(u+v)w=uw+vw
and
(\lambda{u})(\mu{v})=(\lambda\mu)(uv)
. We call an algebra
V
over
\mathbb{C}
a
normed algebra
if for all
u,v\in{V}
we have
\|uv\|\leq\|u\|\|v\|
. We call a normed algebra a
Banach algebra
if it is a Banach space. If
V
is a normed algebra with a multiplicative identity, then we call
V

unital
.
Given
V
is a an algebra, and a vector subspace
W
, then we call
B
a
subalgebra
if
v,w\in{W}
implies
vw\in{W}
.

And if
V
is an algebra that is commutative as a ring, then it is a
commutative algebra
.

We shall assume that our algebras are unital.

We define the
spectrum
of
x
, denoted as
\sigma(x)
, in a Banach algebra
V
as the set of complex numbers
\lambda
such that
x-\lambda{I}
is not invertible, i.e.,
\sigma(x)=\{\lambda\in\mathbb{C}:x-\lambda{I}\text{ is not invertible}\}
.

Proposition F.1
.

The spectrum of an element in a Banach algebra
A
is a non-empty compact subset of
\mathbb{C}
.

Proof sketch.

First start with the
Murray-von Neumann criterion
, which states that for
x
in a Banach algebra
A
, if
\|x\|<1
then
1-x
is invertible.
It then follows that the spectrum of
x
is in fact closed.
Then it follows from Heine-Borel,
\sigma(x)
is compact since it is closed and bounded.

To show that it is non-empty, we need to define the resolvent set of
x

\rho(x)
. This is the complement of the spectrum
\rho(x)=\mathbb{C}\setminus\sigma(x)
. And we also define the resolvent map of
x
for
\lambda\in\rho(x)
as
R_{\lambda}(x)=(\lambda-x)^{-1}
.

Then it is easy to see that as
\lambda\to\infty
we have
\|R_{\lambda}(x)\|\to 0
.
It is also easy to see that for
\lambda,\mu\in\rho(x)
, we have
R_{\lambda}-R_{\mu}=(\mu-\lambda)R_{\lambda}{R_{\mu}}
.

There is an analogue to Louiville’s theorem for complex functions, so it then follows that the spectrum is non-empty.
∎

F.II
{C^{*}}
-algebras

Definition F.2

(
∗
-algebra)
.

A
∗
-algebra
is an algebra
A
with an involution map
{}^{*}\colon{x}\mapsto{x^{*}}
which for
x,y\in{A}
and
\lambda\in\mathbb{C}
satisfies

(i)

(xy)^{*}=y^{*}x^{*}

(ii)

(x+y)^{*}=x^{*}+y^{*}

(iii)

\lambda^{*}=\bar{\lambda}

(iv)

x^{**}=x

We say a
∗
-algebra is an
abstract

C^{*}
-algebra
if it is a Banach
∗
-algebra where the norm satisfies the
C^{*}
-identity

\|x\|^{2}=\|x^{*}x\|
.

The completion of a Banach algebra with an involution is an abstract
C^{*}
-algebra.

Example F.3
.

The complex numbers
\mathbb{C}
forms a
C^{*}
-algebra, by defining the involution
\lambda^{*}=\overline{\lambda}
and where the norm is
\|\lambda\|=|\lambda|
.

We say that a
∗
-algebra is a
concrete
C^{*}
-algebra
if it is a closed subalgebra of
\mathbb{B}(\mathcal{H})
.

Example F.4
.

So the set of bounded operators on a Hilbert space
\mathcal{H}
,
\mathbb{B}(\mathcal{H})
, is one example of a concrete
C^{*}
-algebra.

Given a
C^{*}
-algebra
A
, if
A
has a unit
1\in{A}
, i.e., an identity element. Then it can easily be shown
1^{*}=1
. This can be seen by
1=(1^{*})^{*}=(1^{*}1)^{*}=(1^{*}(1^{*})^{*})=1^{*}1=1^{*}
.

Proposition F.5
.

Given a
C^{*}
-algebra
A
, the involution is continuous.

Proof.

Let
x_{n}\in{A}
such that
x_{n}\to{x\in{A}}
. So,
\|x_{n}^{*}-x^{*}\|=\|(x_{n}-x)^{*}\|
.
Now we want to show
\|(x_{n}-x)^{*}\|=\|x_{n}-x\|
. So
\|x_{n}-x\|^{2}=\|(x_{n}-x)^{*}(x_{n}-x)\|\leq\|(x_{n}-x)^{*}\|\|x_{n}-x\|
, so if
x_{n}-x\neq 0
then
\|x_{n}-x\|\leq\|(x_{n}-x)^{*}\|
(otherwise if
x_{n}-x=0
, then we are done). So,
\|(x_{n}-x)^{*}\|\leq\|((x_{n}-x)^{*})^{*}\|=\|x_{n}-x\|
. So, then,
\|(x_{n}-x)^{*}\|=\|x_{n}-x\|
.

So, we now have
\|x_{n}^{*}-x^{*}\|=\|x_{n}-x\|\to 0
since
x_{n}\to{x}
. Therefore, the involution is continuous.
∎

Proposition F.6
.

If
A
is a
C^{*}
-algebra, then
\sigma(x^{*})=\sigma(x)
for all
x\in{A}
.

Given a
C^{*}
-algebra
A
, then we have

–

x\in{A}
is
normal
if
xx^{*}=x^{*}x
.

–

y\in{A}
is
Hermitian
if
x=x^{*}
.

–

u\in{A}
is
unitary
if
uu^{*}=u^{*}u=1
.

–

p\in{A}
is a
projection
if
p=p^{*}=p^{2}
.

The following result is left as an exercise to the reader.

Proposition F.7
.

If
x
is an element of a
C^{*}
-algebra
A
. Then
x^{*}x
is Hermitian.

Definition F.8
.

Given
C^{*}
-algebras
A
and
B
, a
∗
-homomorphism
is an algebra homomorphism
\alpha:A\to{B}
such that
\alpha(x^{*})=\alpha(x)^{*}
for all
x\in{A}
. A
∗
-homomorphism,
\alpha
, between unital
C^{*}
-algebras is itself
unital
if
\alpha(1)=1
.

Theorem F.9
.

Any
∗
-homomorphism is continuous, with closed image, and is bounded with norm at most one. Any injective
∗
-homomorphism is an isometry.

So, the norm on a
C^{*}
-algebra is determined by the rest of the algebraic structure.

A
∗
-homomorphism is an
isomorphism
of
C^{*}
-algebras if it is bijective.

Proposition F.10
.

The inverse of a bijective
∗
-homomorphism is also a
∗
-homomorphism.

F.III
Three topologies on
\mathbb{B}(\mathcal{H})

Definition F.11

(WOT, SOT, & norm topology)
.

norm

The
norm topology
on
\mathbb{B}(\mathcal{H})
is given by the norm
\|T\|=\sup_{\|v\|\leq 1}\|T(v)\|
.

WOT

The
weak operator topology
on
\mathbb{B}(\mathcal{H})
is given by

\{b\in\mathbb{B}(\mathcal{H}):|\langle{ax,y}\rangle-\langle{bx,y}\rangle|<\epsilon\text{ where }a\in\mathbb{B}(\mathcal{H}),x,y\in\mathcal{H}\text{ and }\epsilon>0\}

SOT

The
strong operator topology
(SOT) on
\mathbb{B}(\mathcal{H})
is given by

\{b\in\mathbb{B}(\mathcal{H}):\|ax-bx\|<\epsilon\text{ where }a\in\mathbb{B}(\mathcal{H}),x\in\mathcal{H}\text{ and }\epsilon>0\}

So, we then have that the norm topology contains the strong and weak operator topologies, i.e.,
\text{WOT}\prec\text{SOT}\prec\text{the norm topology}
. And so for any
A\subset\mathbb{B}(\mathcal{H})
, we have
\overline{A}^{\|\cdot\|}\subset\overline{A}^{\text{SOT}}\subset\overline{A}^{\text{WOT}}
.

F.IV
von Neumann algebras

Definition F.12

(commutant)
.

We define the
commutant
of
A\subseteq\mathbb{B}(\mathcal{H})
as

A^{\prime}=\{y\in\mathbb{B}(\mathcal{H}):xy=yx\text{ for all }x\in{A}\},

and the
bicommutant
by
A^{\prime\prime}=(A^{\prime})^{\prime}
.

The following theorem is known as the
bicommutant theorem
.

Theorem F.13
.

Let
M\subset\mathbb{B}(\mathcal{H})
be a unital
∗
-subalgebra. Then the following three are equivalent.

(i)

M
is closed in WOT

(ii)

M
is closed in SOT

(iii)

M=M^{\prime\prime}=(M^{\prime})^{\prime}

Definition F.14

(von Neumann algebra)
.

A unital
∗
-subalgebra
M\subseteq\mathbb{B}(\mathcal{H})
is a
von Neumann algebra
if it satisfies any of the properties in the above theorem.

It is clear that any von Neumann algebra is a
C^{*}
-algebra.

Example F.15
.

The set of bounded linear maps on the Hilbert space
\mathbb{B}(\mathcal{H})
is a von Neumann algebra.
We also have
M_{n}(\mathbb{C})
as a von Neumann algebra.

We note that von Neumann algebras come in pairs
M,M^{\prime}
.

F.V
Factors

Definition F.16

(factor)
.

We call a von Neumann algebra
M
a
factor
if
M\cap{M^{\prime}}=\mathbb{C}\cdot 1_{\mathbb{B}(\mathcal{H})}
(i.e., the center is trivial).

Example F.17
.

The set of bounded linear maps on the Hilbert space
\mathbb{B}(\mathcal{H})
is thus also a factor.

The only commutative factor is
\mathbb{C}
.

Given
M
is a von Neumann algebra, then

–

let
e,f\in{M}
be two projections, then
e
and
f
are
equivalent
if there exists
u\in{M}
such that
u^{*}u=e
and
uu^{*}=f
. We write
e\sim{f}
if they are equivalent.

–

let
e,f\in{M}
be two projections, then if there exists
u\in{M}
such that
u^{*}u=e
and
u^{*}uf=u^{*}u
. We write this as
e\preceq{f}
.

–

we say a projection
p\in{M}
such that
p\neq 0
is
minimal
if for all projections
a\in{M}
we have that if
a\leq{p}
then either
a=0
or
a=p
.

–

we say a projection
e\in{M}
is
finite
if we have that for all projections
f\in{M}
, if
e\sim{f}\leq{e}
then
f=e
.

The types of factors
M\subseteq\mathbb{B}(\mathcal{H})
:

–

type
I
factor
if there exists a minimal projection in
M
.

–

we call the factor
M\subseteq\mathbb{B}(\mathcal{H})
a
type
II
factor
if there exists a finite projection in
M
and there does not exist a minimal projection in
M
.

–

given
M\subseteq\mathbb{B}(\mathcal{H})
is a type II factor and
1_{\mathbb{B}(\mathcal{H})}
is finite, then
M
is a
type
II
1

factor
.

–

if
1_{\mathbb{B}(\mathcal{H})}
is infinite and there exists finite projections, then it is said to be a
type
II
∞

factor
.

–

finally, we have that the factor
M\subseteq\mathbb{B}(\mathcal{H})
is a
type
III
factor
if there exists no finite projections in
M
.

We will only discuss type II
1
factors in this paper. So to simplify, a factor is of type II
1
if all projections are finite (i.e.,
1_{\mathbb{B}(\mathcal{H})}
is finite) and there does not exist a minimal projection.

F.VI
Trace

We call a linear functional
f
on a von Neumann algebra
M
,

–

positive
if
f(x^{*}x)\geq 0
for all
x\in{M}
,

–

faithful
if when we have
f(x^{*}x)=0
, then
x=0
,

–

state
if
f(1)=1
, and

–

tracial
if
f(xy)=f(yx)
for all
x,y\in{M}
.

Type II
1
factors
M
admit a unique faithful tracial state
\text{tr}\colon{M\to\mathbb{C}}
, so

(i)

\text{tr}(xy)=\text{tr}(yx)
for all
x,y\in{M}

(ii)

\text{tr}(1)=1

(iii)

\text{tr}(xx^{*})>0
for all
x\in{M}
where
x\neq 0
.

We call a linear functional
\text{tr}\colon{M\to\mathbb{C}}
a
trace
if
\text{tr}(xy)=\text{tr}(yx)
for all
x,y\in{M}
.

Given
M
is a finite factor, now we can say that two projections
e,f\in{M}
are equivalent if
\text{tr}(e)=\text{tr}(f)
.

F.VII
The index theorem

We define a Hilbert space
L^{2}(M,\text{tr}_{M})
to be the completion of
M
with respect to the inner product
\langle{a,b}\rangle=\text{tr}_{M}(b^{*}a)
.

Definition F.18

(Jones index)
.

Given
N
is a subfactor of
M
, we define the
Jones index
of
N
as
[M:N]=\dim_{N}{L^{2}(M,\text{tr}_{M})}
.

Theorem F.19

(index theorem)
.

Given
N
is a II
1
subfactor of
M
, then we have

[M:N]\in\left\{4\cos^{2}(\pi/(n+2)):n\geq 1\right\}\cup[4,\infty).

Jones proved this using the basic construction explained in the following section.

F.VIII
Jones’ basic construction

In this section we will discuss Jones’ basic construction for type II
1
subfactors. This discussion is majorly based on that of Jones’ paper
[
25
]
, Penneys’ lecture notes
[
52
]
, and Speicher’s lecture notes
[
59
]
.

Theorem F.20

(GNS - Gelfand-Naimark-Segal)
.

Every abstract
C^{*}
-algebra is isometrically
∗
-isomorphic to a concrete
C^{*}
-algebra.

Theorem F.21

(GNS construction)
.

Given a unital
C^{*}
-algebra
A
and a state
f\colon{A\to\mathbb{C}}
. There exists a Hilbert space
\mathcal{H}^{\prime}
, a
∗
-homomorphism
\pi\colon{A\to\mathbb{B}(\mathcal{H}^{\prime})}
, and a unit vector
h\in\mathcal{H}^{\prime}
such that for all
a\in{A}
we have
f(a)=\langle\pi(a)h,h\rangle
.

We have the GNS representation of a factor
M
on
L^{2}(M,\text{tr}_{M})
, which is given by
\langle{{x},{y}}\rangle=\text{tr}_{M}(y^{*}x)
.

Since the entire chapter was filled with definition and results, it would be reasonable to summarise what it is exactly we need in order to discuss Jones’ basic construction.

So a von Neumann algebra
A
is a unital
∗
-subalgebra of
\mathbb{B}(\mathcal{H})
such that
A=A^{\prime\prime}
; see Theorem
F.13
. A factor
M
is a von Neumann algebra such that the center is trivial (i.e.,
M\cap{M^{\prime}}=\mathbb{C}\cdot 1_{\mathbb{B}(\mathcal{H})}
). A factor is of type II
1
if it is of infinite dimension and it admits a unique tracial state. We then define a Hilbert space
L^{2}(M,\text{tr}_{M})
to be the completion of
M
with respect to the inner product
\langle{a,b}\rangle=\text{tr}_{M}(b^{*}a)
. So,
M
acts on
L^{2}(M,\text{tr}_{M})
by both left and right multiplication. So, for a projection
p\in{M}
, we have the representation
L^{2}(M,\text{tr}_{M})p
. We then have that for II
1
factors
N\subset{M}
, we have
[M:N]=\dim_{N}(L^{2}(M,\text{tr}_{M}))
.

We have the conjugate-linear unitary functional
J\colon{L^{2}(M,\text{tr}_{M})\to{L^{2}(M,\text{tr}_{M})}}
given by
{x}\mapsto{{x^{*}}}
. Then we have
JM^{\prime}J=M
.

Now consider a subfactor
N\subset{M}
, and the Hilbert space
L^{2}(M,\text{tr}_{M})
. We see that are already five II
1
factors, namely:
M
,
M^{\prime}
,
N
,
N^{\prime}
, and
JNJ
.

Proposition F.22

(
[
25
, pp. 7,8]
)
.

Given finite von Neumann algebras
N\subset{M}
with a faithful normal trace
\text{tr}_{N}
, with
1_{N}=1_{M}
. Then there exists a normal linear map
E_{N}\colon{M\to{N}}
defined by
\text{tr}_{N}(E_{N}(x)y)=\text{tr}_{N}(xy)
for
x\in{M}
and
y\in{N}
, and satisfies the following properties

(i)

E_{N}(axb)=aE_{N}(x)b
for
x\in{M}
and
a,b\in{N}

(ii)

E_{N}(x^{*})=E_{N}(x)^{*}
for all
x\in{M}

(iii)

E_{N}(x^{*})E_{N}(x)\leq{E_{N}(x^{*}x)}
for all
x\in{M}

(iv)

E_{N}(x^{*}x)=0
implies
x=0
for all
x\in{M}

The above proposition essentially says that
E_{N}
is a trace-preserving, faithful and positive linear map. We call
E_{N}
the
conditional expectation
of
M
to
N
.

Proposition F.23

(
[
59
, Proposition 5.4]
)
.

Given II
1
factors
N\subset{M}
, there exists the conditional expectation
E_{N}\colon{M\to{N}}
, and an orthogonal projection
e_{N}\colon{L^{2}(M,\text{tr}_{M})\to{L^{2}(N,\text{tr}_{N})}}
such that

(i)

it is uniquely determined by
e_{N}xe_{N}=E_{N}(x)e_{N}
for
x\in{M}

(ii)

xe_{N}=e_{N}x
if and only if
x\in{N}

(iii)

N=M\cap\{e_{N}\}^{\prime}

Basic construction.

Given II
1
factors
N\subset{M}
.
Let
e_{N}\colon{L^{2}(M,\text{tr}_{M})}\to{L^{2}(N,\text{tr}_{N})}
be an orthogonal projection. Then we have
N=M\cap\{e_{N}\}^{\prime}
. So, a direct corollary to this is that we have the von Neumann algebra
\langle{M,e_{N}}\rangle
on
L^{2}(M,\text{tr}_{M})
which is defined by
(M\cup\{e_{N}\})^{\prime\prime}=JN^{\prime}{J}
. Thus we also have
[M:N]=\text{tr}(e_{N})^{-1}=[\langle{M,e_{N}}\rangle:M]
, where the trace is defined on
\langle{M,e_{N}}\rangle
.

And so analogously to how for a von Neumann algebra
M
there exists a von Neumann algebra
M^{\prime}
;
The basic construction tells us that for a subfactor
N\subset{M}
there exists subfactors
JNJ
and
JN^{\prime}{J}
on
L^{2}(M,\text{tr}_{M})
.

Thus, by iterating the basic construction, we find a tower
M_{i}
of II
1
factors with
M_{0}=N
,
M_{1}=M
and
M_{i+1}=\langle{M_{i},e_{M_{i-1}}}\rangle
.

N\subset{M}\overset{e_{M}}{\subset}M_{2}\overset{e_{M_{2}}}{\subset}\cdots\overset{e_{M_{n}}}{\subset}\langle{M_{n},e_{M_{n}}}\rangle=M_{n+1}\subset\cdots

For better readability, we let
e_{i}=e_{M_{i}}
, and call the sequence of
(e_{i})
the
Jones projections
.

Theorem F.24
.

The Jones projections
(e_{i})
satisfy the following properties.

(i)

\left[M:N\right]e_{i}e_{i\pm 1}e_{i}=e_{i}

(ii)

e_{i}e_{j}=e_{j}e_{i}\text{ if }|i-j|\geq 2

(iii)

e_{i}^{2}=e_{i}^{*}=e_{i}

(iv)

\left[M:N\right]\text{tr}_{n+1}(xe_{n})=tr_{n}(x)\text{ where }x\text{ is a word on }1,e_{1},e_{2},\ldots,e_{n-1}

These relations are similar to those of the braid group and the Markov moves. This is the similarity that Didier Hatt-Arnold pointed out to Vaughan Jones in 1982 (see Introduction
A
).
The reader should instantly notice that the Jones projections
(e_{i})
satisfy the properties of the Temperley-Lieb algebras from Definition
G.5
given
d^{2}=[M:N]
. For instance, for part (i) we have,

\displaystyle[M:N]e_{n}e_{n-1}e_{n}

\displaystyle=[M:N]E_{n}(e_{n-1})e_{n}

\displaystyle=[M:N]\text{tr}_{n+1}(e_{n-1})e_{n}

\displaystyle=[M:N][M:N]^{-1}e_{n}=e_{n}

G
The Temperley-Lieb algebras

The Temperley-Lieb algebra was first introduced in 1971 by Lieb and Temperley
[
42
]
.
In this chapter, we will see the relation between the von Neumann algebra that we constructed in the previous chapter (via the Jones’ projections) and the Temperley-Lieb algebra. This will help our understanding since it can be explained in a diagrammatic setting.

Our discussion will mainly depend on that found in
[
52
]
.

G.I
Quantum integers

Definition G.1
.

A
qunatum integer

[n]_{q}
for
n\in\mathbb{Z}
and
q\in\{Q\cup-Q\}
where
Q:=\{e^{i\theta}:\theta\in(0,\pi/2)\}\cup[1,\infty)
, is defined as
\dfrac{q^{n}-q^{-n}}{q-q^{-1}}
.

A quantum integer is essentially a deformation of an integer by
q
.

Example G.2
.

So the quantum integer
[1]_{q}
is
1
, while
[2]_{q}=q+q^{-1}
.

Proposition G.3
.

We can double a quantum integer,
[2]_{q}[n]_{q}=[n+1]_{q}+[n-1]_{q}
.

Proof.

\displaystyle[2]_{q}[n]_{q}

\displaystyle=\frac{(q+q^{-1})(q^{n}-q^{-n})}{q-q^{-1}}

\displaystyle=\frac{q^{n+1}-q^{1-n}+q^{n-1}-q^{-n-1}}{q-q^{-1}}

\displaystyle=\frac{q^{n+1}-q^{-(n+1)}}{q-q^{-1}}+\frac{q^{n-1}-q^{-(n-1)}}{q-q^{-1}}

And so the result then follows.
∎

Proposition G.4
.

Given
m\geq{a}
, we have
[m-a]_{q}=[m]_{q}[a+1]_{q}-[m+1]_{q}[a]_{q}
.

Proof.

\displaystyle[m-a]_{q}

\displaystyle=\frac{q^{m-a}-q^{a-m}}{q-q^{-1}}

\displaystyle=\frac{(q^{m-a}-q^{a-m})(q-q^{-1})}{(q-q^{-1})(q-q^{-1})}

\displaystyle=\frac{q^{m-a+1}-q^{m-a-1}-q^{a-m+1}+q^{a-m-1}}{q^{2}+q^{-2}}

\displaystyle=\frac{q^{m+a+1}-q^{m+a+1}+q^{-m-a-1}-q^{-a-m-1}+q^{m-a+1}-q^{m-a-1}-q^{a-m+1}+q^{a-m-1}}{q^{2}+q^{-2}}

\displaystyle=\frac{q^{m+(a+1)}-q^{m-(a+1)}-q^{(a+1)-m}+q^{-m-(a+1)}}{q^{2}+q^{-2}}

\displaystyle\qquad\quad-\frac{q^{a+(m+1)}-q^{-a+(m+1)}-q^{a-(m+1)}+q^{-a-(m+1)}}{q^{2}+q^{-2}}

\displaystyle=\left(\frac{q^{m}-q^{-m}}{q-q^{-1}}\right)\frac{q^{a+1}-q^{-(a+1)}}{q-q^{-1}}-\left(\frac{q^{m+1}-q^{-(m+1)}}{q-q^{-1}}\right)\frac{q^{a}-q^{-a}}{q-q^{-1}}

\displaystyle=[m]_{q}[a+1]_{q}-[m+1]_{q}[a]_{q}

∎

G.II
Defining the Temperley-Lieb algebra
{TL_{n}}

Definition G.5
.

For
d\in\{Q\cup-Q\}
,
TL_{n}(d)
is the associative unital (i.e., has an identity)
*
-algebra with generators
e_{1},e_{2},\ldots,e_{n-1}
and relations

(i)

e_{i}^{2}=e_{i}=e_{i}^{*}

(ii)

e_{i}e_{j}=e_{j}e_{i}
for
|i-j|\geq 2

(iii)

e_{i}e_{i\pm 1}e_{i}=d^{-2}{e_{i}}
.

So we can reduce each word in the algebra with the relations.

Example G.6
.

So,
TL_{1}
is generated by
1
,
TL_{2}
is generated by
1
and
e_{1}
,
TL_{3}
is generated by
1
,
e_{1}
,
e_{2}
,
e_{1}e_{2}
and
e_{2}e_{1}
, and so on.

Definition G.7
.

The
n
-th
Catalan number

c_{n}
is given by
\dfrac{1}{n+1}\left(\!\!\!\begin{array}[]{c}2n\\
n\end{array}\!\!\!\right)
.

In our above example, we saw
\dim(TL_{1})=1=c_{1}
,
\dim(TL_{2})=2=c_{2}
and
\dim(TL_{3})=5=c_{3}
. So, we have the following result.

Proposition G.8
.

TL_{n}
is finite dimensional.

Sketch of Proof.

Essentially, since this is a finitely generated group. We have any word in the algebra can be written as

(e_{i_{1}}e_{i_{1}-1}\cdots{e_{k_{1}}})(e_{i_{2}}e_{i_{2}-1}\cdots{e_{k_{2}}})\cdots(e_{i_{p}}e_{i_{p}-1}\cdots{e_{k_{p}}})

for
1\leq{i_{1}}<i_{2}<\cdots<i_{p}
and for
1\leq{k_{1}}<k_{2}<\cdots<k_{p}
.
Thus the dimension is less than or equal to the
n^{\text{th}}
Catalan number.

\dim(TL_{n})\leq{c_{n}}

∎

It is easy to realise that this is essentially the type II
1
algebra formed from the Jones projections
(e_{i})
in the previous chapter.

G.III
Diagrammatic definition of the Temperley-Lieb algebra
gTL_{n}

We now discuss the diagrammatic definition of the Temperley-Lieb algebras. This will help us in the construction of the Jones polynomial in the next chapter.

Definition G.9
.

For
d\in\{Q\cup-Q\}
, we call the algebra
gTL_{n}(d)
the
Temperley-Lieb algebra
, whose basis is the set of non-intersecting string diagrams on a rectangle with
n
boundary points on the top and bottom.
The multiplication is defined by concatenation
gTL_{n}\times{gTL_{n}}\to{gTL_{n}}

\cdots
\cdots
x
\cdot
\cdots
\cdots
y
=
\cdots
\cdots
\cdots
x
y

If a closed loop appears in the diagram, we can remove it by multiplying the diagram by the weight of the closed loop (which is
d
).

We have that two elements in
gTL_{n}
are equivalent if the strings are ambient isotopic. So by holding all the boundary points in place, we can move the strings around, given that they do not intersect or break the definition.

Thus the relations for our generators in
gTL_{n}
are

(i)

E_{i}^{2}=dE_{i}=dE_{i}^{*}

(ii)

E_{i}E_{j}=E_{j}E_{i}
for
|i-j|\geq 2

(iii)

E_{i}E_{i\pm 1}E_{i}=E_{i}

These relations are closely related to that of
TL_{n}
. One can define a homomorphism by mapping
e_{i}

d^{-1}E_{i}
. In fact,
gTL_{n}
is
∗
-isomorphic to
TL_{n}
.

Theorem G.12
.

There exists a
∗
-isomorphism from
TL_{n}
to
gTL_{n}
.

So from this point forth, we denote
\mathcal{TL}_{n}
as our Temperley-Lieb algebra, where we will use the diagrammatic definition. So we have the generators
E_{i}
for
i=1,2,\ldots,n-1
and the relations above.

It is typical to wonder whether the conditional expectation on
\mathcal{TL}_{n}
defined above is related to the conditional expectation on factors in the previous chapter. This would make sense as to why we started with von Neumann algebras before defining the Temperley-Lieb algebras. The following proposition will answer our question.

Proposition G.14
.

There exists the following relations,

(i)

\mathcal{E}_{n+1}\circ{i_{n}}=d\cdot\text{id}_{n}

(ii)

\text{tr}_{n+1}=tr_{n}\circ\mathcal{E}_{n+1}

(iii)

(i_{n}\circ{i_{n-1}}\circ\mathcal{E}_{n}(x))E_{n}=E_{n}i_{n}(x)E_{n}
for all
x\in\mathcal{TL}_{n}

(iv)

\text{tr}_{n}(xy)=\text{tr}_{n}(yx)
for all
x,y\in\mathcal{TL}_{n}

(v)

\text{tr}_{n+1}(i_{n}(x)\cdot{E_{n}})=\text{tr}_{n}(x)
for all
x\in\mathcal{TL}_{n}

(vi)

\text{tr}_{n}(\mathcal{E}_{n+1}(x)\cdot{y})=\text{tr}_{n+1}(x\cdot{i_{n}(y)})
for all
x\in\mathcal{TL}_{n+1}
and
y\in\mathcal{TL}_{n}

(vii)

\text{tr}_{n}(1_{n})=d^{n}

(iii)

i_{n}\circ{i_{n-1}}\circ\mathcal{E}_{n}(x)
,

x
\cdots
\cdots

and so, multiplying by
E_{n}
gives

x
\cdots
\cdots
.
.
.
.

This can be seen to be the same as
E_{n}i_{n}(x)E_{n}
,

x
\cdots
\cdots
.
.
.
.
.
.
.
.

Therefore, we can see that for any
x\in\mathcal{TL}_{n}
, we have
E_{n}i_{n}(x)E_{n}=(i_{n}\circ{i_{n-1}}\circ\mathcal{E}_{n}(x))E_{n}
.

Remark
.

Now comparing the above relations and the relations found in Propositions
F.22
and
F.23
, we find that they are related. For instance, in factors
N\subset{M}
, we know
\text{tr}_{M}(E_{N}(x))=\text{tr}_{N}(x)
for all
x\in{N}
where
E_{N}\colon{N}\to{M}
. This is the same as (ii) in the above proposition.
This means that the conditional expectation on factors is related to the conditional expectation on
\mathcal{TL}_{n}
, and the Jones projections are related to the generators on
\mathcal{TL}_{n}
. But to relate one to the other, we must be extra careful with the inclusion map on
\mathcal{TL}_{n}
. For instance, part (iii) above is similar to the relation in part (i) of Proposition
F.23
.

The trace on
\mathcal{TL}_{n}
is called the
Markov trace
, and is unique up to a scalar (the scalar being
d^{n}
).

Remark
.

To get a normal trace, i.e.,
\text{tr}_{n}(1)=1
. We need to define the trace as the number of loops minus
n
. So, then it is clear that we would get:
\text{tr}_{n}(1)=1
;
\text{tr}_{n}(xy)=\text{tr}_{n}(yx)
; and
\text{tr}_{n+1}(xE_{n})=d^{-1}\text{tr}_{n}(x)
for all
x,y\in\mathcal{TL}_{n}
.
We will not use the normal trace, since we will normalise our Jones polynomial in the following chapter.
So this is only an interesting remark and nothing else.

G.V
The Jones-Wenzl idempotents

In this section we will discuss the Jones-Wenzl idempotents. We say an element is an idempotent if when multiplied by itself it equals itself. So any identity is itself an idempotent.
We now let
[n]_{q}=[n]
, for better readability.

Proposition G.15
.

Suppose there exists
f^{(n)}\in\mathcal{TL}_{n}
such that
f^{(n)}\neq 0
,
(f^{(n)})^{2}=f^{(n)}
and for all
i=1,\ldots,n-1
we have
E_{i}f^{(n)}=f^{(n)}E_{i}
. Then
f^{(n)}
is unique for each
\mathcal{TL}_{n}
.

Proof.

Let
f_{1}^{(n)},f^{(n)}\in\mathcal{TL}_{n}
satisfy all properties and
f_{1}^{(n)}\neq{f^{(n)}}
.
So by writing them as a linear combination of the generators
\{1,E_{1},\ldots,E_{n-1}\}
we have

f^{(n)}=x+\sum_{i}{y_{i}E_{i}}\qquad\qquad{f_{1}^{(n)}}=x^{\prime}+\sum_{i}{y^{\prime}_{i}E_{i}}

It then follows that
x=x^{\prime}=1
. Since both are idempotents we then have,

\displaystyle f^{(n)}

\displaystyle=f^{(n)}f_{1}^{(n)}

\displaystyle=\left(1+\sum_{i}{y_{i}E_{i}}\right)f_{1}^{(n)}

Now
\left(\sum_{i}y_{i}E_{i}\right)f_{1}^{(n)}=0
, and so the result then follows, i.e.,
f^{(n)}=f_{1}^{(n)}
.
∎

Definition G.16

(Jones-Wenzl idempotents
[
52
, p. 30]
)
.

The
Jones-Wenzl idempotents
are
f^{\left(n\right)}\in\mathcal{TL}_{n}
are defined inductively such that

(i)

f^{\left(0\right)}\in\mathcal{TL}_{0}
. is the empty diagram

(ii)

f^{\left(1\right)}\in\mathcal{TL}_{1}
is the single strand

(iii)

if
[n+1]\neq 0
, then

f^{(n+1)}=i_{n}\left(f^{(n)}\right)-\frac{[n]}{[n+1]}i_{n}\left(f^{(n)}\right)E_{n}i_{n}\left(f^{(n)}\right).

To understand this better, we will need to use the diagrams. So,
f^{(n+1)}
can be rewritten as,

Proposition G.18

(
[
52
, p. 31]
)
.

Suppose
n\geq 0
and
[1],\ldots,[n],[n+1]\neq 0
so
f^{\left(0\right)},\ldots,f^{\left(n+1\right)}
are well-defined. Then,
f^{\left(n+1\right)}
satisfies the following.

(i)

f^{\left(n+1\right)}=\left(f^{\left(n+1\right)}\right)^{*}=\left(f^{\left(n+1\right)}\right)^{2}

(ii)

\mathcal{E}_{n+1}\left(f^{\left(n+1\right)}\right)=\dfrac{[n+2]}{[n+1]}f^{\left(n\right)}

(iii)

\left(i_{n}\left(f^{\left(n\right)}\right)\right)f^{\left(n+1\right)}=f^{\left(n+1\right)}\left(i_{n}\left(f^{\left(n\right)}\right)\right)=f^{\left(n+1\right)}

(iv)

\text{tr}_{n+1}\left(f_{\left(n+1\right)}\right)=[n+2]

(v)

E_{j}f^{(n+1)}=f^{(n+1)}E_{j}=0
for all
j=\{1,\ldots,n\}

Proof.

We show this by induction on
n
.
This is obvious for
n=0
.
So suppose this is true for any
n
. Then, we need to show that it is also true for
n+1
.

\lxSVG@closescope {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}\hss}\lxSVG@discardpath\lxSVG@closescope \hss}}\lxSVG@closescope\endpgfpicture}}

And again by the inductive hypothesis, we know
f^{(n)}\left(i_{n-1}\left(f^{(n-1)}\right)\right)=\left(i_{n-1}\left(f^{(n-1)}\right)\right)f^{(n)}=f^{(n)}
. And so by stretching the
E_{n}
loops, it is easy to see that we get the same diagram as the second term. Equivalently we can use Proposition
G.14
to see (our last diagram)

i_{n}\left(f^{(n)}\right)E_{n}f^{(n-1)}E_{n}i_{n}\left(f^{(n)}\right)
is equivalent to
i_{n}\left(f^{(n)}\right)E_{n}i_{n}\left(f^{(n)}\right)
. Thus by further simplifying, we find that it is in fact idempotent, i.e.,
\left(f^{(n+1)}\right)^{2}=f^{(n+1)}
.

(ii)

We will now use the results from Proposition
G.14
. So,

\displaystyle\mathcal{E}_{n+1}\left(f^{(n+1)}\right)

\displaystyle=\mathcal{E}_{n+1}\left(i_{n}\left(f^{(n)}\right)-\frac{[n]}{[n+1]}i_{n}\left(f^{(n)}\right)E_{n}i_{n}\left(f^{(n)}\right)\right)

\displaystyle=[2]\text{id}_{n}\left(f^{(n)}\right)+\frac{[n]}{[n+1]}f^{(n)}f^{(n)}

\displaystyle=[2]f^{(n)}+\frac{[n]}{[n+1]}f^{(n)}

and using the result “doubling the quantum integer” from Proposition
G.3
, we find
[2][n+1]=[n+2]+[n]
, and so the result becomes
\dfrac{[n+2]}{[n+1]}f^{(n)}
.

(iii)

We use the results from Proposition
G.14
,

\displaystyle f^{(n+1)}\left(i_{n}\left(f^{(n)}\right)\right)

\displaystyle=\left(i_{n}\left(f^{(n)}\right)-\frac{[n]}{[n+1]}i_{n}\left(f^{(n)}\right)E_{n}i_{n}\left(f^{(n)}\right)\right)\left(i_{n}\left(f^{(n)}\right)\right)

\displaystyle=\left(i_{n}\left(f^{(n)}\right)\right)\left(i_{n}\left(f^{(n)}\right)\right)-\frac{[n]}{[n+1]}i_{n}\left(f^{(n)}\right)E_{n}i_{n}\left(f^{(n)}\right)i_{n}\left(f^{(n)}\right)

\displaystyle=i_{n}\left(f^{(n)}\right)-\frac{[n]}{[n+1]}i_{n}\left(f^{(n)}\right)E_{n}i_{n}\left(f^{(n)}\right)

\displaystyle=f^{(n+1)}

(iv)

Now from (ii), we have
\mathcal{E}_{n+1}\left(f^{(n+1)}\right)=\dfrac{[n+2]}{[n+1]}f^{(n)}
. So, then since
\text{tr}_{n}\circ\mathcal{E}_{n+1}=\text{tr}_{n+1}
, we have

\text{tr}_{n+1}\left(f^{(n+1)}\right)=\text{tr}_{n}\circ\mathcal{E}_{n+1}\left(f^{(n+1)}\right)=\frac{[n+2]}{[n+1]}\text{tr}_{n}\left(f^{(n)}\right)

and by the inductive hypothesis, we have
\text{tr}_{n}\left(f^{(n)}\right)=[n+1]
, and so

\text{tr}_{n+1}\left(f^{(n+1)}\right)=[n+2]

(v)

Finally, by the inductive hypothesis, for any
j=1,\ldots{n-1}
we have
E_{j}f^{(n+1)}=f^{(n+1)}E_{j}
. So let
j=n
, then

E_{n}f^{(n+1)}=E_{n}i_{n}\left(f^{(n)}\right)-\frac{[n]}{[n+1]}E_{n}i_{n}\left(f^{(n)}\right)E_{n}i_{n}\left(f^{(n)}\right)

So, from Proposition
G.14
, we have
E_{n}i_{n}\left(f^{(n)}\right)E_{n}=\left(i_{n}\circ{i_{n-1}}\circ\mathcal{E}_{n}\left(f^{(n)}\right)\right)E_{n}
. And from (ii) we know
\mathcal{E}_{n}\left(f^{(n)}\right)=\dfrac{[n+1]}{[n]}f^{(n-1)}
, so then

\displaystyle E_{n}f^{(n+1)}

\displaystyle=E_{n}i_{n}\left(f^{(n)}\right)-\frac{[n]}{[n+1]}\left(i_{n}\circ{i_{n-1}}\circ\mathcal{E}_{n}\left(f^{(n)}\right)\right)E_{n}i_{n}\left(f^{(n)}\right)

\displaystyle=E_{n}i_{n}\left(f^{(n)}\right)-\left(i_{n}\circ{i_{n-1}}\left(f^{(n-1)}\right)\right)E_{n}i_{n}\left(f^{(n)}\right)

Now we have
i_{n}\circ{i_{n-1}}\left(f^{(n-1)}\right)E_{n}i_{n}\left(f^{(n)}\right)
is equivalent to
E_{n}i_{n}\left(f^{(n)}\right)
, and so the result then follows.

∎

Theorem G.19

(
[
52
, p. 31]
)
.

Suppose
\text{tr}_{j}(y^{*}x)
is positive and semi-definite (i.e.,
\text{tr}_{j}(x^{*}x)\geq 0
and
\text{tr}_{j}(x^{*}x)=0
if and only if
x^{*}x=0
) for all
j\geq 0
,
x,y\in\mathcal{TL}_{n}
. Then

q+q^{-1}\in\left\{2\cos(\pi/n):n\geq 3\right\}\cup[2,\infty)

Proof.

We show this by contradiction. We will assume
q+q^{-1}\not\in\{2\cos(\pi/n):n\geq 3\}\cup[2,\infty)
. Using our Jones-Wenzl idempotents, we want to show that
\text{tr}_{j}((f^{(w)})^{*}f^{(w)})=[w+1]<0
for some
w
.

If we let
q=e^{i\theta}
for some
\theta\in(0,\pi/2)
such that
\theta\neq\pi/n
for some
\pi\geq 3
, then by recalling
\sin(x)=\dfrac{e^{ix}-e^{-ix}}{2i}
, we have

[j]=\frac{(e^{i\theta})^{j}-(e^{i\theta})^{-j}}{(e^{i\theta})-(e^{-i\theta})}=\frac{\sin(j\theta)}{\sin(\theta)}

Now by letting
k\geq 2
be minimal such that
\theta>\pi/(k+1)
, we have

\frac{\pi}{k}>\theta>\frac{\pi}{k+1}

then since
\sin(\theta),\sin(2\theta),\ldots,\sin(k\theta)>0
but we have
\sin((k+1)\theta)<0
so then
[1],[2],\ldots,[k]>0
, but
[k+1]<0
.

So since
k\geq 2
and
[1],[2],\ldots,[k]\neq 0
we have our idempotents
f^{(0)},\ldots,f^{(k)}
are well-defined. Thus, we get our contradiction by taking the trace
\text{tr}_{k}\left({(f^{(k)})^{*}f^{(k)}}\right)=[k+1]<0
.
∎

To get invariance under conjugation (the Markov
M1
move), we need to define a trace. To define a trace, we need a representation of
\mathcal{B}_{n}
in a type II
1
factor since it is not finite (recall the motivation section §
E.I
).

Proposition H.1
.

The homomorphism
\phi_{n}\colon\mathbb{C}[\mathcal{B}_{n}]\to\mathcal{TL}_{n}
which is defined by

\phi_{n}(\sigma_{i})=A(1_{n})+A^{-1}E_{i}\quad\mbox{ and }\quad\phi_{n}(\sigma^{-1}_{i})=A^{-1}(1_{n})+AE_{i},

is a representation of
\mathcal{B}_{n}
(i.e., the homomorphism preserves the structure of
\mathcal{B}_{n}
), where
d=([2]_{q})_{-A^{2}=q}
.

Proof.

If
|i-j|\geq 2
, then

\displaystyle\phi_{n}(\sigma_{i}\sigma_{j})

\displaystyle=\phi_{n}(\sigma_{i})\phi_{n}(\sigma_{j})

\displaystyle=(A(1_{n})+A^{-1}E_{i})(A(1_{n})+A^{-1}E_{j})

\displaystyle=A^{2}+E_{j}+E_{i}+A^{-2}E_{i}E_{j}

\displaystyle=(A(1_{n})+A^{-1}E_{j})(A(1_{n})+A^{-1}E_{i})

\displaystyle=\phi_{n}(\sigma_{j})\phi_{n}(\sigma_{i})

\displaystyle=\phi_{n}(\sigma_{j}\sigma_{i})

since if
|i=j|>1
, then
E_{i}E_{j}=E_{j}E_{i}
.

\displaystyle\phi_{n}(\sigma_{i}\sigma_{i+1}\sigma_{i})

\displaystyle=\phi_{n}(\sigma_{i})\phi_{n}(\sigma_{i+1})\phi_{n}(\sigma_{i})

\displaystyle=(A(1_{n})+A^{-1}E_{i})(A(1_{n})+A^{-1}E_{i+1})(A(1_{n})+A^{-1}E_{i})

\displaystyle=(A^{2}+E_{i+1}+E_{i}+A^{-2}E_{i}E_{i+1})(A(1_{n})+A^{-1}E_{i})

\displaystyle=A^{3}+2AE_{i}+AE_{i+1}+A^{-1}E_{i+1}E_{i}+A^{-1}E^{2}_{i}+A^{-1}E_{i}E_{i+1}+A^{-3}E_{i}E_{i+1}E_{i}

\displaystyle=A^{3}+2AE_{i}+AE_{i+1}+A^{-1}E_{i+1}E_{i}+A^{-1}d{E_{i}}+A^{-1}E_{i}E_{i+1}+A^{-3}{E_{i}}

\displaystyle=A^{3}+E_{i}(2A+A^{-1}d+A^{-3})+AE_{i+1}+A^{-1}E_{i+1}E_{i}+A^{-1}E_{i}E_{i+1}

Note that

\phi_{n}(\sigma_{i+1}\sigma_{i}\sigma_{i+1})=A^{3}+E_{i+1}(2A+A^{-1}d+A^{-3})+AE_{i}+A^{-1}E_{i}E_{i+1}+A^{-1}E_{i+1}E_{i}

So, we need
d=-A^{2}-A^{-2}=([2]_{q})_{-A^{2}=q}
.

Now

\displaystyle\phi_{n}(\sigma_{i})\phi_{n}(\sigma_{i}^{-1})

\displaystyle=(A(1_{n})+A^{-1}E_{i})(A^{-1}(1_{n})+AE_{i})

\displaystyle=1_{n}+A^{2}E_{i}+A^{-2}E_{i}+E_{i}^{2}

\displaystyle=1_{n}+E_{i}(A^{2}+A^{-2})+d{E_{i}}=1_{n}

∎

Proposition H.2
.

And

\displaystyle\text{tr}_{n}\circ\phi_{n}\left(\mathinner{\mathchoice{\vrule width=0.0pt,height=10.0pt,depth=5.0pt\begin{picture}(-3.0,-1.0)\Line(-3,3)(3,-3)\Line(-3,-3)(-.5,-.5)\Line(3,3)(.5,.5)\end{picture}}{\vrule width=0.0pt,height=7.5pt,depth=2.5pt\begin{picture}(-2.0,-1.0)\Line(-2,2)(2,-2)\Line(-2,-2)(-.5,-.5)\Line(2,2)(.5,.5)\end{picture}}{\vrule width=0.0pt,height=7.5pt,depth=2.5pt\begin{picture}(-2.0,-1.0)\Line(-2,2)(2,-2)\Line(-2,-2)(-.5,-.5)\Line(2,2)(.5,.5)\end{picture}}{\vrule width=0.0pt,height=7.5pt,depth=2.5pt\begin{picture}(-2.0,-1.0)\Line(-2,2)(2,-2)\Line(-2,-2)(-.5,-.5)\Line(2,2)(.5,.5)\end{picture}}}\right)

∎

Now
d^{-1}\text{tr}_{n}\circ\phi_{n}
is in fact the braid analog of the Kauffman bracket. This can easily be seen with the state sum solution. The states of a braid closure is given by resolving the crossings in the braid, then taking the trace. Thus

\langle{\hbox{\hskip Thus we can then define the Jones polynomial to be the braid analog of the Kauffman bracket multiplied by
(-A^{-3})^{\omega(\hbox{\hskip 336.20482pt})}
.

However, we want to show that it is indeed a link invariant without the Kauffman bracket.
So we have the identity map of a braid
\text{id}_{n}\colon\mathcal{B}_{n}\to\mathcal{B}_{n}
. Note that we have the following relations,

(i)

\phi_{n+1}\circ\text{incl}_{n}(\alpha)=i_{n}\circ\phi_{n}(\alpha)
, where
\alpha\in\mathcal{B}_{n}

(ii)

\text{id}_{n}\circ\phi_{n}(\alpha)=\phi_{n}\circ\text{id}_{n}(\alpha)
, where
\alpha\in\mathcal{B}_{n}

This is true since, for instance, in the first relation, the inclusion of a braid would not change the
\mathcal{TL}_{n}
representation. We draw the first relation,

So we can thus use the relations from Proposition
G.14
.

Since any braid word
\alpha\in\mathcal{B}_{n}
can be written with braid generators, we have the
writhe
defined on braids as the sum of the exponents of the generators.

\omega(\sigma_{1}^{i_{1}}\sigma_{2}^{i_{2}}\cdots\sigma_{n-1}^{i_{j}})=\sum_{z}i_{z}

Equivalently, the writhe could also be defined as the writhe of the closure of the braid since an orientation is given with the braid closure.

Theorem H.3

(The original Jones polynomial)
.

For a braid
b\in\mathcal{B}_{n}
. We can define the Jones polynomial link invariant as the following

V(L)=V(\hbox{\hskip 441.65944pt\hskip-2.14583pt\hbox{$b$}\hskip-2.14583pt\hskip-441.65944pt\raisebox{17.94456pt}{\hbox{$\hbox{\raisebox{-3.34055pt}{\resizebox{52312104}{141084}{\hbox{\raisebox{10.00012pt}{$\mathchoice{\raisebox{-853.45891pt}{\resizebox{468892385}{36044800}{\hbox{\raisebox{10.00012pt}{$\displaystyle\mathchoice{\raisebox{0.0pt}{\resizebox{0}{0}{\hbox{\raisebox{10.00012pt}{$\displaystyle\kern-0.6pt\bigwedge\kern-0.6pt$}}}}}{\raisebox{0.0pt}{\resizebox{0}{0}{\hbox{\raisebox{10.00012pt}{$\textstyle\kern-0.6pt\bigwedge\kern-0.6pt$}}}}}{\raisebox{0.0pt}{\resizebox{0}{0}{\hbox{\raisebox{1.4pt}{$\scriptstyle\kern-0.6pt\bigwedge\kern-0.6pt$}}}}}{\raisebox{0.0pt}{\resizebox{0}{0}{\hbox{\raisebox{1.0pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle\kern-0.6pt\bigwedge\kern-0.6pt$}}}}}$}}}}}{\raisebox{-853.45891pt}{\resizebox{468892385}{36044800}{\hbox{\raisebox{10.00012pt}{$\textstyle\mathchoice{\raisebox{0.0pt}{\resizebox{0}{0}{\hbox{\raisebox{10.00012pt}{$\displaystyle\kern-0.6pt\bigwedge\kern-0.6pt$}}}}}{\raisebox{0.0pt}{\resizebox{0}{0}{\hbox{\raisebox{10.00012pt}{$\textstyle\kern-0.6pt\bigwedge\kern-0.6pt$}}}}}{\raisebox{0.0pt}{\resizebox{0}{0}{\hbox{\raisebox{1.4pt}{$\scriptstyle\kern-0.6pt\bigwedge\kern-0.6pt$}}}}}{\raisebox{0.0pt}{\resizebox{0}{0}{\hbox{\raisebox{1.0pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle\kern-0.6pt\bigwedge\kern-0.6pt$}}}}}$}}}}}{\raisebox{-157.14236pt}{\resizebox{468892385}{36044800}{\hbox{\raisebox{1.4pt}{$\scriptstyle\mathchoice{\raisebox{0.0pt}{\resizebox{0}{0}{\hbox{\raisebox{1.4pt}{$\displaystyle\kern-0.6pt\bigwedge\kern-0.6pt$}}}}}{\raisebox{0.0pt}{\resizebox{0}{0}{\hbox{\raisebox{1.4pt}{$\textstyle\kern-0.6pt\bigwedge\kern-0.6pt$}}}}}{\raisebox{0.0pt}{\resizebox{0}{0}{\hbox{\raisebox{0.98pt}{$\scriptstyle\kern-0.6pt\bigwedge\kern-0.6pt$}}}}}{\raisebox{0.0pt}{\resizebox{0}{0}{\hbox{\raisebox{0.7pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle\kern-0.6pt\bigwedge\kern-0.6pt$}}}}}$}}}}}{\raisebox{-157.14285pt}{\resizebox{468892385}{36044800}{\hbox{\raisebox{1.0pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle\mathchoice{\raisebox{0.0pt}{\res 441.65944pt})=\frac{(-A^{-3})^{\omega(b)}\text{tr}_{n}\circ\phi_{n}(b)}{d}.

Proof.

We will prove this in two ways for the sake of argument and not necessity.

We will first show that this is in fact an invariant under the Markov moves, which in turn shows that this is invariant under the Reidemeister moves, making it a link invariant. And the second proof will show that this is obviously equivalent to our definitions of the Jones polynomial (Definition
C.11
& Proposition
C.20
).

Invariance under Markov moves:

M1

Given any braid
\gamma\in\mathcal{B}_{n}
, we have
\omega(\gamma)=-\omega(\gamma^{-1})
. So
\omega(\gamma{b}\gamma^{-1})=\omega(\gamma)+\omega(b)+\omega(\gamma^{-1})=\omega(b)
. So,

\displaystyle=\frac{(-A^{-3})^{\omega(b\sigma_{n})}\text{tr}_{n+1}\circ\phi_{n+1}(\text{incl}_{n}(b)\sigma_{n})}{d}

\displaystyle=\frac{(-A^{-3})^{\omega(b)+1}\text{tr}_{n+1}(\phi_{n+1}(\text{incl}_{n}(b))(A+A^{-1}E_{n}))}{d}

.

. So, then

Skein relation:

Let us now ensure that this satisfies the skein relation definition.
Consider single crossings in the braid closure,

\displaystyle A^{4}V\left(\mathinner{\mathchoice{\vrule width=0.0pt,height=10.0pt,depth=5.0pt\begin{picture}(-3.0,-1.0)\Line(-3,-3)(3,3)\Line(-3,3)(-.5,.5)\Line(3,-3)(.5,-.5)\end{picture}}{\vrule width=0.0pt,height=7.5pt,depth=2.5pt\begin{picture}(-2.0,-1.0)\Line(-2,-2)(2,2)\Line(-2,2)(-.5,.5)\Line(2,-2)(.5,-.5)\end{picture}}{\vrule width=0.0pt,height=7.5pt,depth=2.5pt\begin{picture}(-2.0,-1.0)\Line(-2,-2)(2,2)\Line(-2,2)(-.5,.5)\Line(2,-2)(.5,-.5)\end{picture}}{\vrule width=0.0pt,height=7.5pt,depth=2.5pt\begin{picture}(-2.0,-1.0)\Line(-2,-2)(2,2)\Line(-2,2)(-.5,.5)\Line(2,-2)(.5,-.5)\end{picture}}}\right)-A^{-4}V\left(\mathinner{\mathchoice{\vrule width=0.0pt,height=10.0pt,depth=5.0pt\begin{picture}(-3.0,-1.0)\Line(-3,3)(3,-3)\Line(-3,-3)(-.5,-.5)\Line(3,3)(.5,.5)\end{picture}}{\vrule width=0.0pt,height=7.5pt,depth=2.5pt\begin{picture}(-2.0,-1.0)\Line(-2,2)(2,-2)\Line(-2,-2)(-.5,-.5)\Line(2,2)(.5,.5)\end{picture}}{\vrule width=0.0pt,height=7.5pt,depth=2.5pt\begin{picture}(-2.0,-1.0)\Line(-2,2)(2,-2)\Line(-2,-2)(-.5,-.5)\Line(2,2)(.5,.5)\end{picture}}{\vrule width=0.0pt,height=7.5pt,depth=2.5pt\begin{picture}(-2.0,-1.0)\Line(-2,2)(2,-2)\Line(-2,-2)(-.5,-.5)\Line(2,2)(.5,.5)\end{picture}}}\right)+(A^{2}-A^{-2})V\left(\mathinner{\mathchoice{\vrule width=0.0pt,height=10.0pt,depth=5.0pt\begin{picture}(-3.0,-1.0)\cbezier(-3,-3)(0,0)(0,0)(-3,3)\cbezier(3,-3)(0,0)(0,0)(3,3)\end{picture}}{\vrule width=0.0pt,height=7.5pt,depth=2.5pt\begin{picture}(-2.0,-1.0)\cbezier(-2,-2)(0,0)(0,0)(-2,2)\cbezier(2,-2)(0,0)(0,0)(2,2)\end{picture}}{\vrule width=0.0pt,height=7.5pt,depth=2.5pt\begin{picture}(-2.0,-1.0)\cbezier(-2,-2)(0,0)(0,0)(-2,2)\cbezier(2,-2)(0,0)(0,0)(2,2)\end{picture}}{\vrule width=0.0pt,height=7.5pt,depth=2.5pt\begin{picture}(-2.0,-1.0)\cbezier(-2,-2)(0,0)(0,0)(-2,2)\cbezier(2,-2)(0,0)(0,0)(2,2)\end{picture}}}\right)

\displaystyle=A^{4}\frac{(-A^{-3})(-A^{3}d)}{d}

\displaystyle\qquad-A^{-4}\frac{(-A^{-3})^{-1}(-A^{-3}d)}{d}+(A^{2}-A^{-2})\frac{d^{2}}{d}

\displaystyle=A^{4}-A^{-4}+(A^{2}-A^{-2})(-A^{-2}-A^{2})=0.

This completes the proof.
∎

Example H.4
.

For example, recall that the closure of
\sigma_{1}^{3}
is equivalent to the right-handed trefoil knot, while
\sigma_{1}^{-3}
is equivalent to the left-handed trefoil knot.

We can see then, that

\displaystyle V(3_{1})

\displaystyle=V(\hbox{\hskip 451.29065pt\hskip-5.10013pt\hbox{$\sigma_{1}^{3}$}\hskip-5.10013pt\hskip-451.29065pt\raisebox{19.14015pt}{\hbox{$\hbox{\raisebox{-3.34055pt}{\resizebox{53617400}{141084}{\hbox{\raisebox{10.00012pt}{$\mathchoice{\raisebox{-853.45891pt}{\resizebox{468892385}{36044800}{\hbox{\raisebox{10.00012pt}{$\displaystyle\mathchoice{\raisebox{0.0pt}{\resizebox{0}{0}{\hbox{\raisebox{10.00012pt}{$\displaystyle\kern-0.6pt\bigwedge\kern-0.6pt$}}}}}{\raisebox{0.0pt}{\resizebox{0}{0}{\hbox{\raisebox{10.00012pt}{$\textstyle\kern-0.6pt\bigwedge\kern-0.6pt$}}}}}{\raisebox{0.0pt}{\resizebox{0}{0}{\hbox{\raisebox{1.4pt}{$\scriptstyle\kern-0.6pt\bigwedge\kern-0.6pt$}}}}}{\raisebox{0.0pt}{\resizebox{0}{0}{\hbox{\raisebox{1.0pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle\kern-0.6pt\bigwedge\kern-0.6pt$}}}}}$}}}}}{\raisebox{-853.45891pt}{\resizebox{468892385}{36044800}{\hbox{\raisebox{10.00012pt}{$\textstyle\mathchoice{\raisebox{0.0pt}{\resizebox{0}{0}{\hbox{\raisebox{10.00012pt}{$\displaystyle\kern-0.6pt\bigwedge\kern-0.6pt$}}}}}{\raisebox{0.0pt}{\resizebox{0}{0}{\hbox{\raisebox{10.00012pt}{$\textstyle\kern-0.6pt\bigwedge\kern-0.6pt$}}}}}{\raisebox{0.0pt}{\resizebox{0}{0}{\hbox{\raisebox{1.4pt}{$\scriptstyle\kern-0.6pt\bigwedge\kern-0.6pt$}}}}}{\raisebox{0.0pt}{\resizebox{0}{0}{\hbox{\raisebox{1.0pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle\kern-0.6pt\bigwedge\kern-0.6pt$}}}}}$}}}}}{\raisebox{-157.14236pt}{\resizebox{468892385}{36044800}{\hbox{\raisebox{1.4pt}{$\scriptstyle\mathchoice{\raisebox{0.0pt}{\resizebox{0}{0}{\hbox{\raisebox{1.4pt}{$\displaystyle\kern-0.6pt\bigwedge\kern-0.6pt$}}}}}{\raisebox{0.0pt}{\resizebox{0}{0}{\hbox{\raisebox{1.4pt}{$\textstyle\kern-0.6pt\bigwedge\kern-0.6pt$}}}}}{\raisebox{0.0pt}{\resizebox{0}{0}{\hbox{\raisebox{0.98pt}{$\scriptstyle\kern-0.6pt\bigwedge\kern-0.6pt$}}}}}{\raisebox{0.0pt}{\resizebox{0}{0}{\hbox{\raisebox{0.7pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle\kern-0.6pt\bigwedge\kern-0.6pt$}}}}}$}}}}}{\raisebox{-157.14285pt}{\resizebox{468892385}{36044800}{\hbox{\raisebox{1.0pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle\mathchoice{\raisebox{0.0pt}{\resizebox{0}{0}{\hbox{\raisebox{1.0pt}{$\displaystyle\kern-0.6pt\bigwedge\kern-0.6pt$}}}}}{\raisebox{0.0pt}{\resizebox{0}{0}{\hbox{\raisebox{1.0pt}{$\textstyle\kern-0.6pt\bigwedge\kern-0.6pt$}}}}}{\raisebox{0.0pt}{\resizebox{0}{0}{\hbox{\raisebox{0.7pt}{$\scriptstyle\kern-0.6pt\bigwedge\kern-0.6pt$}}}}}{\raisebox{0.0pt}{\resizebox{0}{0}{\hbox{\raisebox{0.5pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle\kern-0.6pt\bigwedge\kern-0.6pt$}}}}}$}}}}}$}}}}}$}}\hskip-451.29065pt\hskip 451.29065pt})

\displaystyle=\frac{(-A^{-3})^{3}\text{tr}_{2}\circ\phi_{2}(\sigma_{1}^{3})}{d}=\frac{-A^{-9}\text{tr}_{2}(\phi_{2}(\sigma_{1})^{3})}{d}

\displaystyle=\frac{-A^{-9}\text{tr}_{2}(A+A^{-1}E_{1})^{3}}{d}

\displaystyle=\frac{-A^{-9}\text{tr}_{2}(A^{3}+3AE_{1}+3A^{-1}E_{1}^{2}+A^{-3}E_{1}^{3})}{d}

\displaystyle=\frac{-A^{-9}(A^{3}d^{2}+3Ad+3A^{-1}d^{2}+A^{-3}d^{3})}{d}

\displaystyle=-A^{-6}d-3A^{-8}-3A^{-10}d-A^{-12}d^{2}

\displaystyle=(-A^{2}-A^{-2})(-A^{-6}-3A^{-10}-A^{-12}(-A^{2}-A^{-2}))-3A^{-8}

\displaystyle=A^{-4}+A^{-12}-A^{-16}

It is clear that the left-handed trefoil
V(\overline{3_{1}})=V(\hbox{\hskip 451.29065pt\hskip-6.44736pt\hbox{$\sigma_{1}^{-3}$}\hskip-6.44736pt\hskip-451.29065pt\raisebox{19.14015pt}{\hbox{$\hbox{\raisebox{-3.34055pt}{\resizebox{53617400}{141084}{\hbox{\raisebox{10.00012pt}{$\mathchoice{\raisebox{-853.45891pt}{\resizebox{468892385}{36044800}{\hbox{\raisebox{10.00012pt}{$\displaystyle\mathchoice{\raisebox{0.0pt}{\resizebox{0}{0}{\hbox{\raisebox{10.00012pt}{$\displaystyle\kern-0.6pt\bigwedge\kern-0.6pt$}}}}}{\raisebox{0.0pt}{\resizebox{0}{0}{\hbox{\raisebox{10.00012pt}{$\textstyle\kern-0.6pt\bigwedge\kern-0.6pt$}}}}}{\raisebox{0.0pt}{\resizebox{0}{0}{\hbox{\raisebox{1.4pt}{$\scriptstyle\kern-0.6pt\bigwedge\kern-0.6pt$}}}}}{\raisebox{0.0pt}{\resizebox{0}{0}{\hbox{\raisebox{1.0pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle\kern-0.6pt\bigwedge\kern-0.6pt$}}}}}$}}}}}{\raisebox{-853.45891pt}{\resizebox{468892385}{36044800}{\hbox{\raisebox{10.00012pt}{$\textstyle\mathchoice{\raisebox{0.0pt}{\resizebox{0}{0}{\hbox{\raisebox{10.00012pt}{$\displaystyle\kern-0.6pt\bigwedge\kern-0.6pt$}}}}}{\raisebox{0.0pt}{\resizebox{0}{0}{\hbox{\raisebox{10.00012pt}{$\textstyle\kern-0.6pt\bigwedge\kern-0.6pt$}}}}}{\raisebox{0.0pt}{\resizebox{0}{0}{\hbox{\raisebox{1.4pt}{$\scriptstyle\kern-0.6pt\bigwedge\kern-0.6pt$}}}}}{\raisebox{0.0pt}{\resizebox{0}{0}{\hbox{\raisebox{1.0pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle\kern-0.6pt\bigwedge\kern-0.6pt$}}}}}$}}}}}{\raisebox{-157.14236pt}{\resizebox{468892385}{36044800}{\hbox{\raisebox{1.4pt}{$\scriptstyle\mathchoice{\raisebox{0.0pt}{\resizebox{0}{0}{\hbox{\raisebox{1.4pt}{$\displaystyle\kern-0.6pt\bigwedge\kern-0.6pt$}}}}}{\raisebox{0.0pt}{\resizebox{0}{0}{\hbox{\raisebox{1.4pt}{$\textstyle\kern-0.6pt\bigwedge\kern-0.6pt$}}}}}{\raisebox{0.0pt}{\resizebox{0}{0}{\hbox{\raisebox{0.98pt}{$\scriptstyle\kern-0.6pt\bigwedge\kern-0.6pt$}}}}}{\raisebox{0.0pt}{\resizebox{0}{0}{\hbox{\raisebox{0.7pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle\kern-0.6pt\bigwedge\kern-0.6pt$}}}}}$}}}}}{\raisebox{-157.14285pt}{\resizebox{468892385}{36044800}{\hbox{\raisebox{1.0pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle\mathchoice{\raiseb 451.29065pt})
, and the bracket polynomial would be
\phi_{2}(\sigma_{1}^{-1})^{3}=(AE_{1}+A^{-1})^{3}=A^{3}E_{1}^{3}+3AE_{1}^{2}+3A^{-1}E_{1}+A^{-3}
, and the Markov trace of the bracket polynomial becomes
A^{3}d^{3}+3Ad^{2}+3A^{-1}d+A^{-3}d^{2}
. And finally we have the Jones polynomial,
V(\overline{3_{1}})=-A^{9}(d(A^{3}d+3A+A^{-3})+3A^{-1}
, which further simplified turns out to be
A^{4}+A^{12}-A^{16}
.

To conclude, we see that the easiest to define (i.e., via the Kauffman bracket) is not necessarily the easiest to work with, while the most difficult to define (i.e., the original construction) is perhaps the easiest to work with.

H.I
Proving Theorem
C.22

In this section we will prove
V(L_{1}\cup{L_{2}})=dV(L_{1})V(L_{2})
and
V(L_{1}\#L_{2})=V(L_{1})V(L_{2})
, where
\#
is the connected sum of the links. We will prove these results using braid representations instead of the skein relation and Kauffman bracket (where they can be derived easily). The reason we do this with braid representations is so that we can ensure comprehension.

We saw in Chapter
D
, that the braid inclusion map essentially adds a strand to the right. So now we define the braid left-inclusion map
\text{lfincl}_{n}
. The reason for this is to define the tensor product of two braids.

Definition H.5

.

The
braid left-inclusion map

\text{lfincl}_{n}\colon\mathcal{B}_{n}\to\mathcal{B}_{n+1}
for
n\geq 1
is defined by,

Figure H-i:
left inclusion
\text{lfincl}_{n}
on
\mathcal{B}_{n}

We similarly define the
left-inclusion
on
\mathcal{TL}_{n}
, i.e.,
li\colon\mathcal{TL}_{n}\to\mathcal{TL}_{n+1}
.

Definition H.6

(braid tensor product)
.

Let
\alpha\in\mathcal{B}_{n}
and
\beta\in\mathcal{B}_{m}
. We define the
tensor product

\otimes\colon\mathcal{B}_{n}\times\mathcal{B}_{m}\to\mathcal{B}_{n+m}
by
\alpha\otimes\beta\mapsto\text{incl}_{n\otimes{m}}(\alpha)\cdot\text{lfincl}_{m\otimes{n}}(\beta)
, where the inclusion tensor product of the two integers is given by
\text{incl}_{n\otimes{m}}=\text{incl}_{n+m-1}\circ\text{incl}_{n+m-2}\circ\cdots\circ\text{incl}_{n}
(the left inclusion is defined analogously). And so we thus have.

\cdots
\cdots
\alpha
\otimes
\cdots
\cdots
\beta
=
\cdots
\cdots
\alpha
\cdots
\cdots
\beta

Figure H-ii:
braid tensor product

Remark
.

It is easy to see that the union of two closure braids is well-defined, i.e.,
\hbox{\hskip .

We then analogously define the
tensor product
on
\mathcal{TL}_{n}
, i.e.,
\otimes\colon{\mathcal{TL}_{n}\times{\mathcal{TL}_{m}}}\to{\mathcal{TL}_{n+m}}
,
\cdots
\cdots
x
\otimes
\cdots
\cdots
y
=
\cdots
\cdots
x
\cdots
\cdots
y

We have the relation
\phi_{n+m}(\alpha\otimes\beta)=\phi_{n}(\alpha)\otimes\phi_{m}(\beta)
, where
\alpha\in\mathcal{B}_{n}
and
\beta\in\mathcal{B}_{m}
. This obviously says something along the lines of, “if two braids are disjoint, then so are their Temperley-Lieb representations”.

Lemma H.7
.

Let
\alpha\in\mathcal{B}_{n}
and
\beta\in\mathcal{B}_{m}
, then we have
\text{tr}_{n+m}\circ\phi_{n+m}(\alpha\otimes\beta)=\text{tr}_{n}\circ\phi_{n}(\alpha)\cdot\text{tr}_{m}\circ\phi_{m}(\beta)
.

Proof sketch.

The diagrammatic sketch of this is pretty straight forward. Essentially, we need to show that the trace of disjoint
\mathcal{TL}
diagrams are independent of each other. Note the relation above,
\phi_{n+m}(\alpha\otimes\beta)=\phi_{n}(\alpha)\otimes\phi_{m}(\beta)
.
\cdots
\cdots
x
\otimes
\cdots
\cdots
y
=
\cdots
\cdots
\phi_{n}(\alpha)
\cdots
\cdots
\phi_{m}(\beta)

Which is clearly the same as
\text{tr}_{n}\circ\phi_{n}(\alpha)\cdot\text{tr}_{m}\circ\phi_{m}(\beta)
.
∎

Definition H.8

(connected sum of links)
.

L_{1}\#L_{2}
is the
connected sum
of the links, and is shown below

\#
L_{1}
L_{2}
=
L_{1}
L_{2}

Figure H-iii:
connected sum of links
\#

It is easy to see that this is well-defined.

An almost direct corollary one can make is the following.

Corollary H.9
.

For links
L_{1},L_{2}
, we have
V(L_{1}\#L_{2})=V(L_{1})V(L_{2})
.

Proof.

We “glue” our link diagrams such that
T_{+}\sim{T_{-}}\sim{L_{1}\#{L_{2}}}
.
L_{1}
L_{2}
T_{+}
L_{1}
L_{2}
T_{-}
L_{1}
L_{2}
T_{0}

It is clear that we have
T_{0}\sim{L_{1}\cup{L_{2}}}
, so then

\displaystyle V(L_{1}\#L_{2})(t^{-1}-t)+d(t^{-1/2}-t^{1/2})V(L_{1})V(L_{2})

\displaystyle=0

And so
V(L_{1}\#L_{2})=V(L_{1})V(L_{2})
.
∎

Now we will see all the different possibilities connecting
E_{n}
, by only looking at the connection between the four points. The first possibility, for instance, gives
.
.
.
.

So, the trace of
\phi_{n+m}(\alpha\otimes\beta)
without
E_{n}
would give
d^{2}
(multiplied by the rest of the diagram), whereas
E_{n}\phi_{n+m}(\alpha\otimes\beta)
gives
d
(multiplied by the rest of the diagram).
The second and third possibilities are the same, but with opposite choices. So without loss of generality, we have,
.
.
.
.

This clearly becomes a single strand.
So the trace would give
d
. Whereas, the trace of
\phi_{n+m}(\alpha\otimes\beta)
without
E_{n}
would give
d^{2}
.
We also have,
.
.
.
.

Similarly to the previous possibilities, we have the trace of
E_{n}\phi_{n+m}(\alpha\otimes\beta)
giving
d
, and
d^{2}
for the trace of
\phi_{n+m}(\alpha\otimes\beta)
without
E_{n}
. We then have two other possibilities (i.e., both strands in a diagram are going down/up and all strands are going down/up) - the reader is advised to try them.

We see that it will always give us
\text{tr}_{n+m}(E_{n}\phi_{n+m}(\alpha\otimes\beta))=d^{-1}\text{tr}_{n+m}\circ\phi_{n+m}(\alpha\otimes\beta)
. So then we have

\text{tr}_{n+m}(E_{n}\phi_{n+m}(\alpha\otimes\beta))=d^{-1}\cdot\text{tr}_{n+m}\circ\phi_{n+m}(\alpha\otimes\beta)

The result then follows,

\displaystyle V(\hbox{\hskip \displaystyle=\frac{(-A^{-3})^{\omega(\alpha)+\omega(\beta)+1}\text{tr}_{n+m}\circ\phi_{n+m}(\alpha\otimes\beta)(A+A^{-1}d^{-1})}{d}
